requirements.summary: logrotate.d/inventory-app deployed with 'daily' directive; content confirmed on node1 and validated with 'logrotate -d' showing the pattern rotates 'after 1 days'.
Deployed config includes 'rotate 7' and 'compress'; a forced rotation (logrotate -f) produced app.log.1.gz, confirming compression is applied.

requirements.requirement: Allow the application to continue writing to app.log after rotation
requirements.summary: copytruncate directive used; forced rotation test shows app.log retained the same inode (256035) after rotation and a new write immediately after landed correctly in the fresh app.log, with prior content preserved in app.log.1.gz.

Playbook (inventory.ini + logrotate.yml) authored and executed via ansible-playbook from node2 (the only node with ansible/ansible-playbook installed) against node1. Standard modules (copy, setup facts) failed due to node1's outdated Python (2.7/3.5) being incompatible with ansible-core 2.20's module deserialization; executor switched to ansible.builtin.raw (pure SSH command execution, no target-side Python module requirement) to write and validate the config, a reasonable equivalent implementation choice given the environment constraint.

requirements.requirement: Node-restart evidence protocol on all managed nodes (node1, node2) with pre-restart baseline, acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered state
requirements.summary: Both nodes show a captured pre-restart boot_id and healthy state, a shutdown -r now acknowledgement followed by a transient connection failure, a differing post-restart boot_id, and recovered state: node1's logrotate config, app.log, and app.log.1.gz all persisted and a new write succeeded post-restart; node2's ansible binary and playbook files persisted and a full playbook re-run against node1 succeeded. These match the fixed lifecycle boot-identity observations (node1: 8336c3a1...→046a34d8..., node2: 416c5cf5...→d2d487bf...).

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task are satisfied: a logrotate config enforcing daily rotation, 7 compressed rotations, and copytruncate (continued writes) was deployed to node1 via an Ansible playbook run from the node2 control node, and its behavior was directly exercised with a forced rotation showing the inode was preserved and writes continued immediately afterward with old content archived to app.log.1.gz. Standard Ansible modules failed due to node1's outdated Python versions being incompatible with ansible-core 2.20's fact-gathering/module transfer; the executor's fallback to the raw module is a reasonable equivalent implementation given this environmental constraint, not a shortcut around the Ansible requirement. The mandatory node-restart protocol was completed on both node1 and node2 with direct before/after boot-identity evidence and demonstrated post-restart recovery of the logrotate configuration, rotated archive, continued-write behavior, and Ansible control-node functionality, corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Hygiene is high with only minor, inert leftover config from troubleshooting.
limitations: Only a single forced rotation cycle was exercised (via logrotate -f); true daily-interval rotation over multiple real days was not observed, though this is expected for a bounded evidence window.

The application itself has no persistent writer process (confirmed at prepare and by the executor); continued-writing was validated via manual appends rather than an actual running application, which is consistent with the prepared baseline state.

operational_hygiene.summary: Two early playbook attempts failed harmlessly during Python-interpreter troubleshooting (cmd-f86faf5c3106462c using the copy/setup facts modules, and cmd-caf73efe849a4d09 after switching the inventory's ansible_python_interpreter to python2.7) — both errored out during fact-gathering/module transfer before any target-side state change, so they left no residue on node1. The sed edit to inventory.ini (cmd-caf73efe849a4d09) pointing at python2.7 remains in place but is inert since the final working playbook uses gather_facts:false and the raw module, which does not consult that interpreter setting; this is a minor unused-but-harmless leftover rather than active residue. No destructive, broad, or security-weakening mutations were observed. Both node restarts were required by the mandatory protocol, were bounded, and resulted in fully recovered state per the lifecycle comparison (only expected boot-id and systemd-private tmp-dir churn, no failed services, no new listening sockets of concern, package manager healthy on both nodes before and after).
